__data__.text: After Parasurama's departure, Rama, now calm, entrusted Viṣṇu's bow to Varuna, the god of water.  He then respectfully addressed the sages, led by Vasiṣṭha, and informed his father, Dasaratha, who was unaware of Parasurama's peaceful exit, that Parasurama had left and suggested the army return to Ayodhya.  Dasaratha, overjoyed at this news, embraced Rama. The king then led the army back to the festive capital city of Ayodhya, which was adorned with flags, filled with music, and citizens rejoicing at their king's return. Dasaratha entered his grand palace.  The queens, including Kausalya, Sumitra, and Kaikeyi, prepared to welcome their daughters-in-law.  Sita, Urmila, Mandavi, and Śrutakīrti were led into the palace, where they performed appropriate rituals and ceremonies.  The princesses, dressed in fine silks, enjoyed the company of their husbands. The princes, skilled in weaponry and surrounded by friends and family, served their father.  Sometime later, Dasaratha addressed Bharata.

__data__.text: King Janaka requested Vasistha to conduct the wedding ceremony of Rama. Vasistha, along with other sages, prepared the altar with flowers, golden plates, colorful jars, incense, and various ritualistic items.  He lit the sacred fire and offered oblations.  Sita, adorned in jewels, was brought before the fire, facing Rama. Janaka formally gave Sita to Rama, declaring her his faithful partner and instructing Rama to take her hand in marriage. He assured Rama of Sita's unwavering devotion.  After Janaka transferred consecrated water to Rama, signifying the giving away of Sita, celestial music played and flowers rained down.  Janaka then offered Urmila to Lakshmana, Mandavi to Bharata, and Shrutakirti to Shatrughna.  The four princes took the hands of their respective brides, circled the fire, altar, King Janaka, and the sages, completing the wedding ceremony according to tradition.  Celestial nymphs danced and Gandharvas sang as the princes, with their brides, circled the sacred fire three times, finalizing their marriages.

__data__.text: The four princes, obedient to King Janaka's words and following Vasistha's guidance, took the hands of their respective brides.  They circumambulated the sacred fire, the altar, King Janaka, and the assembled sages, completing the traditional wedding rites.  A magnificent shower of blossoms fell from the sky, accompanied by the resounding beat of celestial drums and the harmonious melodies of vocal and instrumental music.  Celestial nymphs danced gracefully, and Gandharvas sang sweetly, creating a wondrous spectacle at the wedding of these descendants of Raghu.  Amidst this celestial symphony, the princes, radiant with joy, circled the sacred fire three times with their brides, finalizing their marriages.  Afterwards, the newlywed princes and their brides retired to their quarters, followed by King Janaka, the sages, and their relatives, all filled with happiness.

__data__.text: After the wedding ceremonies, Sage Viswamitra departed for the northern mountains. King Dasaratha, after bidding farewell to King Janaka, began his journey back to his capital, Ayodhya.  King Janaka presented a lavish dowry, including riches, textiles, animals, and servants. As Dasaratha journeyed homeward with his sons and their brides, unsettling omens appeared. Fearful birds cried out, while deer crossed their path from the left.  Concerned, Dasaratha questioned Sage Vasistha about these signs. Vasistha explained the bird cries signified imminent danger, while the deer offered some reassurance. As they discussed this, a powerful storm suddenly arose, shaking the earth, uprooting trees, and darkening the sky.

__data__.text: As Dasaratha and his entourage journeyed towards Ayodhya, unsettling omens arose, causing the king to seek Vasistha's counsel.  Vasistha interpreted the ominous bird cries as a sign of impending danger, while the presence of deer offered a glimmer of hope.  Suddenly, a violent storm erupted, plunging the world into darkness and chaos. Amidst this turmoil, a formidable figure emerged, radiating an intense aura. This was Parasurama, the legendary warrior-sage, recognizable by his matted locks and the axe resting on his shoulder. He appeared as imposing as Mount Kailasa and as fierce as the fire of cosmic destruction.  Recognizing the potential threat, Vasistha and the accompanying sages gathered, fearing Parasurama's wrath and a potential repeat of his past actions against the Kshatriya caste.  However, they hoped his previous purge had quenched his anger and grief over his father's death.  To placate the imposing figure, the sages approached Parasurama with offerings of respect, addressing him with reverence.

__data__.text: Parasurama, addressing Rama, recounts Rama's impressive feat of breaking Shiva's bow. He reveals he has brought another sacred bow, inherited from his father Jamadagni, and challenges Rama to string it as a display of strength.  Upon witnessing Rama stringing the bow, Parasurama promises a duel to further test Rama's valor.  King Dasaratha, distressed, pleads with Parasurama to spare his young sons. He reminds Parasurama of his ascetic life and past renunciation of violence after giving up his anger towards Kshatriyas. Dasaratha recounts how Parasurama relinquished his weapons after giving his word to Indra and gifted the earth to Sage Kasyapa before retiring to Mount Mahendra. He emphasizes that their entire family's lives depend on Rama's safety.  Ignoring Dasaratha's pleas, Parasurama continues to address Rama, describing the two divine bows revered by the world, crafted by Vishwakarma.  He explains that Rama broke the first bow, originally given to Shiva for his battle against Tripura. The second bow, wielded by Parasurama, belonged to Vishnu.  Parasurama details how he inherited this powerful bow and, after conquering the earth and giving it to Kasyapa, retreated to Mount Mahendra. Hearing of the broken bow, he returned, driven by his accumulated spiritual energy.  Finally, invoking the Kshatriya duty of accepting a righteous duel, he urges Rama to take up Vishnu's bow.

__data__.text: Parasurama continues his narrative, revealing the origin of the bow he holds. He explains that Rama broke Shiva's bow, originally given to him by the gods for his battle against the demon Tripura.  The bow Parasurama now presents was Vishnu's, bestowed upon him by the gods.  He relates a tale of a conflict between Shiva and Vishnu, instigated by Brahma to test their might. During the battle, Vishnu's roar rendered Shiva's bow useless and Shiva himself immobile. The gods intervened, requesting peace. Witnessing Vishnu's power, they deemed him superior, angering Shiva, who then gave his bow to King Devarata. Vishnu entrusted his bow to Rcika, who passed it down to Jamadagni, Parasurama's father.  Jamadagni, a peaceful sage, had no need for such a weapon. King Arjuna, mistaking Jamadagni's gentle nature for weakness, killed him.  Enraged by this act, Parasurama repeatedly exterminated the Kshatriya caste in revenge.

__data__.text: Parasurama explains that the bow he now possesses, originally Vishnu's, rivals Shiva's bow in power.  He recounts a battle between Shiva and Vishnu where Vishnu's roar disabled Shiva's bow and paralyzed him. The gods intervened, requesting peace. Impressed by Vishnu's might, they declared him superior, angering Shiva who then gave his bow to King Devarata. Vishnu gave his bow to Rcika, who passed it down to Jamadagni, Parasurama's father. King Arjuna, misjudging Jamadagni's peaceful nature, killed him.  Enraged, Parasurama repeatedly annihilated the Kshatriya caste in revenge. After conquering the earth, he gave it to Kasyapa as a sacrificial offering.  Upon hearing of Shiva's bow being broken, he returned. He now challenges Rama to string Vishnu's bow, urging him to uphold the Kshatriya duty of accepting a righteous duel.

__data__.text: Rama, no longer constrained by his father's presence, addressed Parasurama.  He acknowledged Parasurama's actions and the fulfillment of his filial duty.  However, he challenged Parasurama's perceived underestimation of him, inviting him to witness his true power.  Angered, Rama seized Parasurama's bow and arrow, stringing the bow and preparing to fire. He declared his respect for Parasurama as both a Brahmin and a kinsman of Vishwamitra, explaining his reluctance to harm him.  Instead, Rama offered an alternative – to strip Parasurama of his power or his claim to the celestial realms. He emphasized the infallibility of Vishnu's bow.  The gods, rishis, and various celestial beings gathered to observe this extraordinary confrontation. The onlookers were stunned by Rama's display of power, and a now powerless Parasurama gazed at him in wonder.  Disoriented by Rama's brilliance and his own diminished state, Parasurama quietly explained his exile from earth at night, a consequence of a past agreement with Sage Kashyapa.  He requested Rama to spare his ability to move freely and declared his intention to retreat to Mount Mahendra.

__data__.text: Parasurama, humbled and drained of power, softly addressed Rama.  He explained his nocturnal exile from Earth, a consequence of a past agreement with Sage Kashyapa. He requested Rama not to impede his movement and declared his intent to retreat to Mount Mahendra.  He urged Rama to use Vishnu's bow to destroy the celestial realms he had earned through his austerities, emphasizing the infallibility of the weapon and the urgency of the act. Parasurama recognized Rama as the imperishable Lord Vishnu, observing the ease with which Rama wielded Vishnu's bow. He noted the assembled gods witnessing the event.  He stated his lack of shame in his defeat, as it was at the hands of the Lord of the three worlds. He again urged Rama to release the arrow, after which he would depart for Mount Mahendra.  As he spoke, Rama released the arrow, destroying Parasurama's celestial rewards. Parasurama immediately departed for Mount Mahendra. The world was filled with light as the gods and rishis praised Rama.  Parasurama, after circumambulating Rama as a mark of respect, finally departed for his abode on Mount Mahendra.

Their love and admiration for each other deepened over time. Sita, beautiful as a goddess, understood Rama's innermost thoughts and feelings.  Their joyful union was likened to that of Vishnu and Lakshmi.

Canto LXXVI

Fitting the arrow to the bow of Lord Visnu and declaring it as unfailing,
Sri Rama asks Parasurama to point out at whom it may be
discharged, and at the instance of the latter puts an
end to his title to the (ethereal) worlds earned
by him through his austerities. Recognizing
Sri Rama to be no other than Lord Visnu
and taking leave of him, ParaSurama
withdraws to Mount Mahendra
in order to resume
his austerities

Canto LXXVII

On the departure of Paragurama, Sri Rama hands over the bow of Lord Visnu
to Varuna (the god of water) and, sending his army ahead, King Dasaratha
enters Ayodhya. After some days Prince Yudhajit, Bharata’s maternal
